Two examples may be useful here. 1. Abd al-Rahman Badawi in his book Aristotle (Cairo, 1964, 4th ed.). 2. Tayyib Tizini in the work cited above. Badawi, as an idealist thinker, argues that for Aristotle true existence is the existence of essences, and that there is no difference between Plato and Aristotle in their view of the “status of existence” (p. 55). He also says that “the central idea in Aristotle, running through every part of his system, is the idea of matter and form” (p. 282). Tizini, by contrast, as a materialist thinker, argues that Aristotle’s basic principle is the objective, real existence of the material world, and that consciousness—thought or essence—derives from the existence of that material world. Tizini therefore believes that this basic principle in Aristotle must be brought clearly to the foreground, because it is here that Aristotle breaks decisively with Plato’s theory of abstract forms, with “Platonism” itself (p. 101). Tizini further argues that Aristotle’s concept of substance, insofar as it includes the eternity of matter in general, marked a major and fundamental step toward a precise dialectical-materialist concept of matter (p. 121).↩︎

In Marxism, the Leninist theoretical principle for identifying stages in the history of philosophy rests on the idea that philosophical development results from a unity of quantitative and qualitative change—that is, from a unity between gradual development and breaks within that development. Engels explains this unity through the law of the negation of the negation. He writes: “Ancient philosophy was spontaneous materialism. For that reason it could not explain the relation between thought and matter. But the need to clarify this question led to teachings about a soul distinct from the body, then to the claim that the soul was immortal, and finally to spiritualism—that is, the unity of soul and body. In this way ancient materialism was negated by idealism. But idealism itself, in the later development of philosophy, also proved unable to sustain itself, and it too was negated by modern materialism. Modern materialism is therefore a negation of the negation. It is not simply a continuation of ancient materialism. Rather, it adds to the enduring foundations of ancient materialism the whole intellectual content produced by two thousand years of philosophical and natural-scientific development, as well as by the development of history itself over those two thousand years” (Engels). See Anti-Dühring, chapter 12, “Dialectics: Negation of the Negation”; Arabic translation by Fu’ad Ayyub, Dar Dimashq, 1st ed., 1965, pp. 165–166.↩︎

Marxists explain the flourishing of classical German philosophy in the nineteenth century, despite Germany’s economic backwardness compared with other European countries at the time, in two ways. First, they see it as one expression of philosophy’s relative independence from the economic base. Second, they see it as the result of two sets of factors: external European factors and internal German ones. In Germany, quantitative changes were accumulating within a process of development. So although the country’s economic and political conditions were still relatively backward in qualitative terms, there was movement within them: a process of formation through accumulating quantitative changes. These accumulations could then turn into new qualitative forms—political, intellectual, or theoretical.↩︎

Lenin exposed the partisanship of idealist philosophers through concrete examples, despite the many masks behind which their philosophical partisanship could hide. He did this in Materialism and Empirio-Criticism; see especially the chapter “Parties in Philosophy and Philosophical Blockheads,” Arabic translation by Munir Shabak and Fu’ad Ayyub, Dar Dimashq, 1971, 1st ed., pp. 335–355. Lenin described neutrality in philosophy as “a disguised baseness, concealing idealism and fideism” (p. 354). In the conclusion to the book (p. 358), he wrote: “Modern philosophy is partisan, just as it was two thousand years ago, and the two parties struggling against each other are, in essence, materialism and idealism.”↩︎

One feature of historical materialism in Marxist thought is that it is not only a method for interpreting history or the world. It is also a method for changing history and changing the world, unlike the task philosophy set itself before Marxism. This is why Marx, in his remarks on Feuerbach, said that philosophy had interpreted the world, whereas the task now was to change it. Earlier inquiry dealt with interpreting the spiritual or ideal world; now the task was to transform the objective, material world.↩︎

Thales (621–550 BCE) tried to develop a fairly integrated view of the world as a unified material whole. He believed that water was the original basis of everything that exists, and that the earth was a round cylinder resting in water.↩︎
Anaximenes (588–524 BCE) believed that air was the basis of everything that exists, and that all things in the world arise through the condensation and rarefaction of air.↩︎

Anaximander (611–547 BCE) approached the origin of the world differently. He argued that the world’s basis did not lie in a concrete material substance, but in an indeterminate substance he called the apeiron. Existing things arise through the interaction of cold and hot, two inseparable qualities of the infinite apeiron. The apeiron is an abstract category, comparable to the category of matter in Marxism.↩︎

Heraclitus (520–470 BCE). Materialist historians of philosophy associate Heraclitus with the emergence of dialectics as an almost fully developed method for analyzing everything that exists. Lenin believed that Heraclitus expressed some essential points of dialectics very well (Philosophical Notebooks). Heraclitus held that the basis of everything must be material and that fire was the primary material basis. Fire is in constant motion and change, continually coming into being and passing away. He gave a material explanation of the soul. Everything turns into something else according to the law of necessity.↩︎

Democritus (second half of the fifth century BCE), together with Leucippus and Anaxagoras, founded the atomist school. They assumed the existence of an infinite number of indivisible particles moving through empty space. These particles, absolutely dense and differing in shape and size, are atoms; atoms and the void are eternal. Against Zeno, Democritus defended the validity of sensory knowledge without setting it against rational knowledge. Nothing exists in the world except atoms and the void. He held that existence and time are eternal. Everything that exists does so for a cause and by necessity; even chance has a cause. He also explained the existence of the gods in material terms.↩︎

Epicurus (341–270 BCE). His philosophy represents the highest stage in the development of ancient Greek atomism. In his theory of knowledge he takes a sensory approach and begins from materialist positions. Like Democritus, he holds that only atoms and the void exist, and that all things and natural phenomena are different combinations of atoms. Coming into being and passing away are simply processes of atoms joining together and separating. Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing turns into nothing. He went beyond Democritus on the question of the weight of atoms, affirming that atoms have weight. He looked for the source of atomic motion within the atoms themselves—that is, for an internal, self-generated source of material motion. His idea that atoms deviate from a straight path contributed to the development of ancient Greek materialism. He linked happiness to knowledge: there can be no happiness without understanding humanity’s place in the world and freeing people from fear—fear of the gods, death, and an unseen afterlife. He denied that the gods intervene in nature, human destiny, or the world. His school was the last major materialist school of ancient Greek philosophy.↩︎

In the Christian Middle Ages, nominalism and realism were the two main currents within which the various schools of Scholastic philosophy developed. They were the historically distinctive form taken by the struggle between materialism and idealism within that philosophy: nominalism represented the materialist side, while realism represented the idealist side. The nominalists denied the real existence of universals—essences—and affirmed the real existence of individual things, arguing that the universal exists only as a name. The realists, by contrast, held that universals had real existence apart from individual things. Among the best-known representatives of Scholastic realism were John Scotus Eriugena (810–877), followed by the philosopher-theologian Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. Among the best-known nominalists was the French philosopher Roscelin (1050–1120), whose view that the word “universal” is merely a verbal label with no reality of its own is considered one of the earliest expressions of materialist nominalism in medieval Scholasticism. He was followed by English representatives of nominalism, the best known being Duns Scotus (1274–1208), Roger Bacon (1214–1294), and William of Ockham (–1341).↩︎

Lange was a major representative of bourgeois philosophy and a historian of philosophy. He became famous for a work described as the first major study in bourgeois materialist history. In 1866 he published History of Materialism and Critique of Its Importance in the Present Age. It was reissued in 1969, when bourgeois philosophers believed that the study had finally destroyed materialism.↩︎

We use “inclination” and “tendency” as synonyms. They help us distinguish between what is materialist or dialectical in the full modern scientific sense and what has not yet developed all the elements of dialectical materialism, or has not yet reached a firm and consistent materialist position. This is why the title of this book speaks of “materialist tendencies,” even though our research sometimes finds clearly materialist positions on particular philosophical questions in some thinkers from the heritage.↩︎

Calls to break with the Arab cultural heritage appeared in different forms and within different ideological currents. They first appeared in the first third of the twentieth century as calls to replace the Arabic alphabet with the Latin alphabet, gradually cutting people off from that heritage. This appeared in two currents. One was in Lebanon, represented by Father Marun Ghusn and later Sa‘id Aql, and was driven by a sectarian political aim: isolating Lebanon from its Arab surroundings as an expression of the ideology of the colonial Lebanese bourgeoisie. The second appeared in Egypt, represented by Abd al-Aziz Fahmi and Salama Musa. This current expressed the ideology of the emerging Egyptian bourgeoisie, based on an Egyptian nationalism separate from Arab nationalism. The slogan of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution was “Egypt for the Egyptians.” After the Arab-Israeli war of June 1967, the same call appeared in another form, under the claim that the Arab defeat resulted from “civilizational” factors rooted in the country’s “civilizational” backwardness and reflected in the literature of the Arab intellectual heritage itself. This newer form appeared in two ways: in literature and in theoretical thought. It appeared artistically, for example in the poetry of Unsi al-Hajj and Nizar Qabbani, and theoretically in the Kuwait symposium on “The Crisis of Arab Civilizational Development,” held in April 1974; see al-Adab, Beirut, no. 5, 1974. In the papers presented at this symposium, the idea of discarding the heritage appeared only indirectly, and perhaps unintentionally, but the logic of the arguments leads in that direction.↩︎

When we speak of the originality of Arab thought—by which we mean all intellectual work originally written in Arabic, rather than translated into it—we mean that this thought is objectively connected to a particular historical and social reality, which it reflects in its own distinctive ways. We insist on this originality for two reasons. First, to affirm this connection as a methodological principle. Second, to affirm the dialectical unity between originality and contemporaneity, or modernity, and therefore to reject the colonial-bourgeois concept of “modernity” detached from originality. Colonialism spent a long period trying, in the cultural sphere, to implant this concept in the minds of the Arab intelligentsia. Its aim was to make it possible to cut modern Arab thought off from its own history—its originality—and redirect it toward ideological dependence on colonial Western thought.↩︎
